en.title: Marlon James's "The Disappearers" Scorches Jamaican Homophobia
en.summary: Marlon James's latest novel, longlisted for the Booker Prize, delivers a powerful and unflinching look at homophobia in Jamaica. This ambitious, polyphonic epic navigates decades of prejudice and violence against the backdrop of the AIDS era.
en.body:
Marlon James has always been drawn to narratives with a grand sense of sweep, exploring both external journeys and profound internal shifts. His latest novel, **The Disappearers**, longlisted for the Booker Prize, embodies this ambition with a sprawling, 640-page epic that plunges readers into the heart of Aids-era Kingston. It’s a work that is as emotionally resonant as it is exhaustive, roping in excursions to 1950s England and the 2000s United States. The novel’s visceral power stems from its unflinching exposé of Jamaican homophobia, painting a grim picture of a society grappling with deep-seated prejudice.

The narrative’s defining event is a brutal mob attack on eight queer men who had gathered in secret to stage John Herbert’s provocative 1967 play, *Fortune and Men’s Eyes*. This clandestine production aimed to dismantle what director Havelock Titus called “the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality.” As Titus explains, the prison setting, a potent symbol of male institutions, paradoxically becomes a space where “masculine sexualities that could never happen outside in the normal world flourish in there all the time.” This core tension fuels the novel's polyphonic storytelling, weaving together multiple voices and perspectives to create a tapestry of struggle, resilience, and devastating loss.

## A Harrowing Depiction of Prejudice

**The Disappearers** is not a gentle read. It is a scorching, sometimes exhausting, but ultimately triumphant exploration of queer life and the violent backlash it faces. The novel’s scope is immense, traversing geographical and temporal landscapes to contextualize the intense homophobia depicted in Kingston. James masterfully uses the play-within-a-novel to confront the societal myths surrounding masculinity and sexuality in Jamaica, revealing the hypocrisy and danger lurking beneath the surface. The characters’ fight to bring their story to the stage becomes a metaphor for their struggle for visibility and survival in a hostile environment.

## Community and Craft

This novel will undoubtedly resonate deeply with readers passionate about LGBTQ+ narratives and those who admire bold, ambitious literary projects. For fans of Marlon James, **The Disappearers** offers the intricate plotting and thematic depth they’ve come to expect, pushing boundaries with its raw portrayal of trauma and resistance. It speaks to the power of art to challenge oppressive systems and the enduring spirit of communities fighting for recognition. The novel’s exploration of how clandestine spaces become vital hubs for queer expression and survival is particularly poignant, highlighting the courage required to simply exist and create in the face of societal condemnation.

## What's Next

While **The Disappearers** is already garnering significant critical attention, including its Booker Prize longlisting, readers can anticipate further discussions and analyses of its complex themes. As with any major literary release, expect to see it appear on year-end best-of lists and spark conversations within literary circles worldwide.

content_raw: This Booker-listed epic set in Aids-era Kingston is a triumph – bitter, bawdy and ravishingly queer “A sense of sweep,” replied Marlon James, when asked what moves him most in literature. “Sweep isn’t just about external journeys, but internal as well. It can be over years and decades, or across land and sea.” If that explanation is still hazy, pick up his mighty new novel, which is longlisted for this year’s Booker prize and is tirelessly – sometimes exhaustingly – grand and peripatetic. Mounting a grisly exposé of Jamaican homophobia, this polyphonic 640-page doorstopper is an emotionally bruising narrative that roves “uptown, downtown, ghetto and gully” through Aids-era Kingston with sidetrack excursions to 1950s England and a closing leap to 2000s United States. The novel’s defining event is a gruesome mob attack on eight queer men who have clandestinely come together to work on bringing John Herbert’s 1967 gay prison play, Fortune and Men’s Eyes, to the stage. The goal, in the words of director Havelock Titus, is to shatter “the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality”. “Because prison,” he explains, “is the ultimate male institution and yet masculine sexualities that could never happen outside in the normal world flourish in there all the time.” Continue reading...
